title: Karnataka Suspends Food Licences of Amazon, Swiggy Instamart, BigBasket Over Toxic Datura Sales
excerpt: The state's food safety authority found poisonous Datura fruits and seeds listed for human consumption on e-commerce platforms, some carrying FSSAI registration numbers.
body:
• Karnataka's Food Safety and Drug Administration has suspended the food licences of Amazon, Swiggy Instamart, and BigBasket over the sale of toxic Datura fruits and seeds on their platforms.
  • The order, dated August 24, treats e-commerce platforms as Food Business Operators directly liable for unsafe products — not just neutral marketplaces.
  • Amazon did not respond to the inquiry; Swiggy Instamart sought additional time; BigBasket's offer to relabel products as "Not for Human Consumption" was deemed insufficient.
  • The crackdown follows a wave of regulatory action against quick-commerce food safety lapses across Karnataka and Maharashtra in 2026.

Karnataka's Food Safety and Drug Administration Department on August 24 ordered the suspension of food licences held by Amazon, Swiggy Instamart, and BigBasket after an inquiry found toxic Datura fruits and seeds being sold on the platforms for human consumption.

The department acted under the Food Safety and Standards (FSS) Act, 2006, and the FSS Rules, 2011, directing concerned authorities to suspend the platforms' licences until further orders. It also ordered the immediate suspension of licences and registrations held by suppliers and sellers who had been providing the products to the three platforms.

What Is Datura and Why Is It Dangerous?

Datura — known as dhatura in Hindi, thorn apple in English, and umathai in Tamil — is a plant whose fruits and seeds contain tropane alkaloids. These compounds can cause hallucinations, delirium, seizures, coma, and death. While Datura has limited traditional-medicine and religious uses in India, there is no safe dose for consumption as food.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=fy5RsoCcEP0

The department's investigation found that packets of Datura fruits and seeds were being listed for sale on the e-commerce platforms under FSSAI licence or registration numbers — the same certification that signals to buyers that a product has been cleared for consumption. Some of these products were stored in warehouses and made available for online sale and distribution.

"The Datura plant possesses toxic properties, and the consumption of its fruits and seeds may cause serious adverse effects on human health."

— Karnataka Food Safety and Drug Administration

How the Platforms Responded

Representatives of all three companies appeared before the authority during the proceedings, but none satisfied the regulator.

Amazon did not submit a response. Swiggy Instamart requested additional time to provide documents on the action it had taken. BigBasket said it had discontinued the sale of Datura fruits and proposed correcting its labelling to read "Not for Human Consumption" in the future.

The department found all three responses unsatisfactory. It noted that BigBasket's relabelling approach did not address the core issue — a toxic substance had been sold as food under food safety registrations.

Platforms Treated as Liable Food Businesses

The order carries significance beyond the immediate suspension. By acting against the platforms' own licences rather than just the third-party sellers' registrations, Karnataka's food safety authority has treated Amazon, Swiggy Instamart, and BigBasket as Food Business Operators (FBOs) directly responsible for what is sold under their registrations.

Section 26 of the FSS Act places a duty on every FBO to ensure the food it handles is safe, while Section 27 fixes liability on sellers and distributors. The department's approach pushes back against the position quick-commerce platforms typically take — that they are neutral marketplaces connecting buyers to sellers, shielded by intermediary protections under the Information Technology Act.

Part of a Broader Crackdown

The Karnataka order fits a pattern of escalating regulatory action against quick-commerce platforms in 2026. Earlier in August, Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration suspended 14 establishments linked to Blinkit, Zepto, and Instamart after a statewide inspection drive, and sealed a Zepto warehouse in Bengaluru. In June, FSSAI sent Blinkit repeated notices over spoiled-food complaints, holding the company to FBO liability after its shift to an inventory-led model in September 2025.

The central regulator had been laying the groundwork since at least July 2025, when it warned more than 70 e-commerce representatives that every entity in the supply chain carries food-safety liability. In December 2024, FSSAI directed e-commerce FBOs to display sellers' FSSAI numbers and stop listing sellers without valid licences.

What Happens Next

The suspensions remain in place until further orders. The department has directed all three platforms and their sellers to remove every listing, advertisement, and promotional material related to Datura intended for food or human consumption — both online and offline. The suspension can be reconsidered only after the platforms submit compliance reports and receive a hearing from the department.

The case raises questions about the reliability of FSSAI registration numbers as a consumer trust signal, especially on platforms where product listings may not undergo manual safety review before going live. For India's rapidly expanding quick-commerce sector — now handling millions of grocery and food orders daily — the Karnataka order may force a reassessment of how platforms vet the products they list and store.
